Consult Summary:
- Acute onset (today) pleuritic right-sided back pain with shortness of breath, two episodes of hemoptysis and subjective fever in a patient with SLE on methotrexate; clinician arranged urgent face-to-face assessment to exclude pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or SLE-related pulmonary disease.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Acute shortness of breath and pleuritic right-sided back pain with two episodes of coughing up blood today; subjective fever and awareness of heartbeat/palpitations.
- Timeline:
  - 2 weeks: increasing tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance.
  - 1 day (today): acute onset cough, pleuritic right-sided back pain (worse on deep inspiration), two episodes of hemoptysis, felt warm/feverish, palpitations.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Pain worse on deep inspiration and with coughing.
  - No relieving factors reported.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - Cough (with blood-streaking on two occasions).
  - Subjective fever (patient checked with back of hand; no measured temperature recorded).
  - Palpitations / awareness of heart beating.
  - No reported chest trauma, leg swelling, or recent long-haul travel.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - Non-smoker.
  - No known prior venous thromboembolism.
  - No known drug/other allergies.
  - No measured temperature, BP, SpO2, or respiratory rate recorded.
  - No other SLE flare features documented (no rash, hematuria, arthritis reported).
- Patient identifiers: patient initially provided the name "Tracy Chapman" and later identified as "Doris" during the consultation (inconsistency noted in transcript).

Past Medical History:
- Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). No other chronic diagnoses documented.

Medications:
- Methotrexate — dose/route/frequency not documented; last taken this morning.
- No other regular medications reported.
- Allergies: No drug, food, or environmental allergies reported.

Social History:
- Lives alone in a flat.
- Occupation: office-based desk job.
- Smoking: Denies smoking.
- Pets: Has a cat.
- No recent long-haul travel reported.

Family History:
- No family history of venous thromboembolism reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals:
  - Radial pulse counted by patient: ~66–74 bpm (remote self-count). No formal BP, SpO2, respiratory rate, or measured temperature recorded.
- Examination findings (remote/video):
  - Peripheral capillary refill visually appeared normal on video.
  - Throat visual inspection unremarkable.
  - Patient palpated neck and reported no enlarged glands.
- Otherwise: Not recorded (no auscultation or in-person exam performed).

Investigations:
- No investigations performed during consultation.
- Planned/anticipated investigations (from clinician plan and DDx): face-to-face chest auscultation, measurement of BP, pulse, temperature, likely SpO2; possible chest X-ray and additional tests depending on clinical findings (see plan).

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Most likely diagnosis: acute chest infection/pneumonia presenting with cough, pleuritic right-sided pain and hemoptysis — requires in-person assessment.
- Key differential considerations: pulmonary embolism (possible pulmonary infarct), SLE-related pulmonary involvement (lupus pneumonitis or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage). Methotrexate-related pneumonitis or opportunistic infection less likely but possible given immunosuppression.

DDx Integration (brief):
- Community-acquired pneumonia — supporting: acute feverish feeling, cough with hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, clinician impression; opposing: no measured fever, no auscultation or imaging yet.
- Pulmonary embolism (± infarct) — supporting: acute pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, palpitations; opposing: no reported VTE risk factors (no recent long-haul travel/immobility, no prior DVT/PE), pulse remotely not markedly tachycardic, no SpO2/ABG.
- SLE-related pulmonary disease (pneumonitis or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage) — supporting: known SLE and hemoptysis; opposing: no other SLE flare features documented and patient appears hemodynamically stable remotely.
- (No conflicts noted between transcript and DDx.)

Issue 1: Acute respiratory illness — probable community-acquired pneumonia
- Assessment: Presentation most consistent with an acute infective chest process (feverish feeling, productive cough with blood-streaking, pleuritic pain).
- Plan:
  - Arrange urgent face-to-face assessment today (support team to book clinic) for full clinical examination.
  - In clinic: chest auscultation, measure BP, pulse, temperature, respiratory rate and SpO2.
  - If examination and observations support infection: consider starting appropriate antibiotics as per local guidance.
  - Consider chest X-ray if focal signs on exam, if hemoptysis persists, or if not improving on initial management.
  - Safety-net: urgent reassessment or emergency attendance for worsening breathlessness, hypoxia, high fever, syncope, large-volume hemoptysis, or rapid clinical deterioration.

Issue 2: Hemoptysis with consideration of pulmonary embolism/pulmonary infarct
- Assessment: Hemoptysis with acute pleuritic pain raises concern for pulmonary embolus with possible infarction; medium likelihood per DDx given clinical features and SLE (prothrombotic risk).
- Plan:
  - Evaluate for PE if face-to-face assessment raises concern (e.g., hypoxia, tachycardia, pleuritic localized findings, risk factors on review).
  - If PE suspected clinically, consider further investigations per local protocol (e.g., D-dimer and/or CT pulmonary angiography) and urgent management pathway.
  - If hemodynamically unstable or severe hypoxia, arrange immediate emergency transfer.

Issue 3: SLE-related pulmonary involvement and methotrexate-related lung disease / opportunistic infection
- Assessment: SLE can cause pneumonitis or alveolar hemorrhage presenting with hemoptysis and dyspnea; methotrexate carries risk of pneumonitis and immunosuppression increasing infection risk — both are possible contributors.
- Plan:
  - Consider baseline blood tests if indicated (e.g., FBC to assess for anemia or bleeding, inflammatory markers) — to be decided at face-to-face review.
  - If autoimmune pulmonary process or drug-induced pneumonitis suspected, consider prompt specialist input (rheumatology/pulmonology) and additional imaging (chest X-ray/CT) and directed investigations.
  - Review methotrexate timing/last dose and consider holding methotrexate if specialist recommends in the context of significant infection or pulmonary toxicity (discuss with rheumatology).

General plan items:
- Support team to book a same-day face-to-face GP clinic for vitals and chest auscultation (as per clinician instruction).
- Do not start antibiotics remotely; clinician will review in person before prescribing.
- Advise patient to attend emergency services if symptoms acutely worsen (marked SOB, difficulty breathing, syncope, heavy hemoptysis, severe chest pain).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: no formal vital signs recorded (BP, temperature, respiratory rate, SpO2), no laboratory tests or imaging available, no quantified amount of hemoptysis.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none identified; DDx aligns with clinician impression in transcript.
- Transcript quality: consultation audio/video understandable though patient hesitated at times; remote exam limited by the modality (no auscultation or formal vitals).  
- Identifier inconsistency: patient initially gave name "Tracy Chapman" and later identified as "Doris" in the transcript (recorded above).
